summary.text: Gravity is the force that draws material objects toward each other, and it is one of four fundamental interactions.
Newton's law says the pull grows with the masses and shrinks with the square of the distance, while Einstein described gravity as curved spacetime.
Gravity shaped stars and galaxies, controls the orbits of planets and satellites, and gives objects weight at a planet's surface.

facts.label: Newton's law
facts.value: Pull rises with mass, falls with distance squared

facts.label: Falling bodies
facts.value: Same gravitational acceleration for all objects

facts.label: Black hole
facts.value: Nothing, not even light, escapes it

items.prompt: Astronauts far above Earth still feel its pull, only weaker. What does this say about gravity's reach?

options.label: It never ends, but its effects weaken as objects get farther away
It stops completely beyond the top of the atmosphere
It stays the same strength no matter how far away
It reaches only as far as the Moon's orbit

items.explain: Gravity has infinite range although its effects become weaker with distance.

items.prompt: A leaf drifts down much slower than a rock. How did Galileo explain this?

options.label: Heavier objects are always pulled harder
Air resistance slows light, wide objects as they fall
The leaf is attracted to the ground less
Leaves are lifted by a force that rocks lack

items.explain: Galileo showed gravitational acceleration is the same for all objects and blamed air resistance for slowing low-density, high-surface-area objects.

items.prompt: An engineer plans a satellite orbit around Earth. Which description of gravity is good enough?

options.label: A full quantum theory of gravity
Einstein's theory with black hole physics
Newton's law of universal gravitation
Aristotle's idea of natural places

items.explain: For most applications gravity is sufficiently well approximated by Newton's law.

items.prompt: Why do physicists generally ignore gravity when studying how two electrons interact?

options.label: Gravity does not act on anything that small
Gravity there pushes rather than pulls
Electrons are too light to have any weight
Their electrical repulsion is vastly stronger than their gravity

items.explain: The ratio of gravitational attraction to electrical repulsion for two electrons is tiny, so gravity can be neglected for subatomic particles.

items.prompt: In the early universe, what pulled clouds of hydrogen gas together until they formed stars?

options.label: Magnetic pull from the first galaxies
Mutual attraction between the gas and clumps of dark matter
Pressure from light pushing the gas inward
Heat that made the gas shrink on its own

items.explain: Gravitational attraction between hydrogen and dark matter clumps made the gas coalesce, eventually forming stars.

items.prompt: A ball dropped from rest falls a certain distance in one second. By Galileo's finding, how far does it fall in two seconds?

options.label: Twice as far
Three times as far
Four times as far
The same distance again

items.explain: Galileo proved the distance fallen is proportional to the square of the time elapsed.

paragraphs.heading: What gravity is
paragraphs.text: Gravity is one of the four fundamental interactions in physics. It can be described as the force that pulls material objects toward one another. The word comes from the Latin gravitas, meaning weight. Gravity reaches without limit, though its pull gets weaker as objects move farther apart.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's law
paragraphs.text: Newton's law of universal gravitation treats gravity as a pull between any two bodies. The pull grows with the product of their masses and shrinks with the square of the distance between them. Written with the gravitational constant G, it reads F = Gmm^(′)/r² for masses m and m′ a distance r apart. For most purposes this law describes gravity well enough.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein's curved spacetime
paragraphs.text: Gravity is also described by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, put forward in 1915. It explains gravity as a bending of spacetime, caused by mass being spread unevenly. The most extreme bending is a black hole: once past its edge, the event horizon, nothing can get out, not even light. Scientists are still hunting for a theory of quantum gravity that would join gravity with the other fundamental interactions in one framework.

paragraphs.heading: Weak but in charge of the sky
paragraphs.text: Between two electrons, gravity's pull is tiny next to their electric push apart: the ratio is 1 to 4.17×10⁴². So gravity can usually be ignored for particles smaller than atoms. At the scale of astronomical bodies, though, it becomes the most important interaction, steering satellites, planets, stars, galaxies and even light. In the early universe, gravity drew clouds of hydrogen and clumps of dark matter together, and the gas condensed into stars. On larger scales this built galaxies and clusters of galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Gravity on Earth
paragraphs.text: At the surface of a planet such as Earth, gravity pulls toward the planet's centre, changed by the effects of the planet's spin. Here gravity gives objects their weight. It helps explain waves on water and tides raised by the Moon, and it plays a large part in weather. Living things use it too: plants grow guided by it through gravitropism, and it affects how fluids flow around the bodies of many-celled organisms.

paragraphs.heading: One kind of mass
paragraphs.text: Gravity is basic in another way too. The inertial mass in Newton's second law turns out to equal the gravitational mass. This idea, the equivalence principle, has been tested by experiment to better than one part in a trillion.

paragraphs.heading: Falling objects through history
paragraphs.text: Aristotle thought heavier objects should fall faster, which was later shown to be wrong. In 628 CE the Indian astronomer Brahmagupta described gravity as an attractive force pulling things to the Earth, calling it gurutvākarṣaṇ. In 1586 Simon Stevin dropped two cannonballs of different sizes and weights from a tower in Delft and saw them fall at the same rate. Galileo's careful measurements of balls rolling down slopes firmly showed that gravity speeds up all objects equally. He put the slow fall of light, broad objects down to air resistance.
